Serafina looked from one to the other. “Right. You’re actually married. I thought he was one of those men who wear a ring so they look unavailable.”

“Are there men like that?” said Jinx.

“Apparently,” said Raiden.

Jinx turned back to Serafina. “He’s unavailable.”

“I gathered,” said Serafina, grinning.

After that the evening got easier. Serafina talked about the difference between a car that felt fast and one that was, and about Nonna, her grandmother’s red rally hatchback with three hundred thousand kilometres on her, whose original gearbox had been jumping out of third for two months. Her own mechanic wanted to put a new box in. She’d rather die. Jinx asked whether it jumped under load or off the throttle, and whether it went back in clean, and at the end of it Serafina said, “You really know it. Can I bring it to you?”

“Bring the whole assembly. I don’t diagnose from a complaint.”

“Does she let you design things at home?” Serafina asked Raiden.

“He designs,” said Jinx. “I reject.”

“Sometimes,” said Raiden.

“Most of the time.”

“Sounds healthy,” said Serafina.

“It is,” said Raiden, and looked at his wife, and she looked back.

His father never came over. Raiden saw him once across the room by the windows, talking to a minister, and saw his father’s eyes find him, and find the woman beside him, and stay there a moment. Then somebody spoke to Lin Jian and he turned away.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the taxi home she sat with her hand on his thigh and watched the clock on the dashboard. 11:58. He was looking out of the window. She touched the washer on his finger.

“Raiden.”

He turned.

“Happy birthday.”

He looked at the clock. 11:59. Then at her. “You remembered.”

“Of course I remembered.”

“I never told you what I wanted.”

“What do you want?”

He looked at their hands. “You.”

“That’s a terrible answer.”

“It’s the true one,” he said, and she kissed him, and at the next red light kissed him again. “Happy birthday, husband.” His phone buzzed twice. Elowen, wishing him a happy birthday and a good night. And then a number he didn’t know.

Unknown: Serafina Song. Your wife’s terrifying. I like her. Gearbox next week.

He showed Jinx. “Good,” she said. “She’s got a gearbox.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina came on the Wednesday with the gearbox in the back of a van and pointed at him across the shop. “You’re the draftsman.” She pointed at Jinx. “And you’re the meanest engineer in the city.”

“Who told you that?”

“Your husband.”

“I didn’t,” said Raiden.

“Your face did.”

It took Jinx two weeks. The dogs on third had worn from square to rounded, so that under power they pushed themselves apart, and the fork had been hammered trying to hold them; thirty years of a family driving it hard and a granddaughter driving it harder. She found good used gears instead of new ones, because Serafina wanted the car to stay itself, and set the fork true and checked every tolerance and ran it through every gear. When Serafina came to collect it she brought a second box: a close-ratio sequential from the team’s old car, sitting in storage, used but properly kept. “A trade. Your work for this, and whatever difference you think is fair.”

“Why?”

“Because I want someone who understands what she’s working on. And because I’ve seen what you do.” Serafina looked round at the shop, the dyno, the steel, the floor. “This place is something.”

“It’s mine,” said Jinx.

“That’s better still.”

Then Serafina asked whether Jinx could build her something. Not a race bike. A road bike that didn’t look like anything else, fast and exact. It took three months. Jinx sketched round Serafina’s reach and weight and how she sat, tuned the engine for the middle of the rev range, set the suspension for her, and painted the bodywork a deep dark gold that looked almost brown under the shop lights and like old bronze in the sun. Raiden brought coffee and held lights and carried parts, and learned very fast not to touch anything without asking.

She handed it over at a petrol station on the edge of the city at the end of July. Serafina walked round it slowly and swung a leg over and found the levers exactly where her hands went, and the pegs exactly where her feet went, and started it, and blipped it twice, and looked up.

“You remembered the lever reach.”

“Yes.”

“This is perfect.”

“Ride it before you decide.”

Serafina got off and hugged her, hard and sudden, and Jinx went stiff for half a second and then laughed and hugged her back. “Your wife’s terrifying,” Serafina told Raiden over her shoulder. “And very good. You’re both unbearable.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d mentioned the sidecar once. One evening after closing, watching her set up the suspension on an old bike, he’d said, almost to himself, “I’ve always wondered what it would be like to ride beside you. Not behind.”

“You want a sidecar?”

“Maybe. I like being able to see your face.”

She’d laughed and gone back to work, and he hadn’t asked again. She remembered. Once the gold bike had gone, she found a frame. She put the chair on the left, the kerb side, the way the road went here. She designed the mounting and worked out the loads and stiffened the attachment points, and set the bike to lean two degrees away from the chair and the chair wheel a centimetre toe-in, so the whole outfit wouldn’t drift for the gutter. It wasn’t decoration. It was built to carry a person safely: proper brackets, bracing, a wheel that tracked true. She built the seat round him. More leg room than she’d have given anyone else. A backrest. A grab rail. A locker under the seat. A screen low enough that it wouldn’t get in the way of him looking at things. She painted it dark green, and on the side fixed a small brass plate that said ARCHITECT.

She finished it on the morning of Saturday the tenth of September and texted him.

Jinx: Petrol station. Bring your helmet.

Raiden: Is something wrong?

Jinx: No.

Raiden: Are you sure?

Jinx: Raiden.

Raiden: Coming.

He stopped at the edge of the forecourt when he saw it. He walked round it slowly, his eyes going over the brackets and the suspension and the seat, and then he saw the brass plate and stopped.

“You built this?”

“Unless you know another idiot called Architect.”

He touched the letters with his thumb. “There’s a backrest. And a rail. And somewhere to put things.”

“I thought of everything you’d complain about.”

He laughed, and then he didn’t, and he pulled her into his arms on the forecourt under the strip lights and held her very tightly with his face in her hair. “Thank you,” he said. And again. “Thank you.”

“Happy birthday,” she said into his shoulder. “Late.”

“My birthday was five months ago.”

“I know.”

She strapped him in and checked the rail and swung onto the bike and looked round. “Ready?”

“Always.”

She let the clutch out and the sidecar came with them, smooth as anything, and he laughed out loud. Not politely, not quietly. The same helpless laugh as the first time on the back of her bike, when he’d begged her for the long way. She heard it over the engine, and took the long way home.

That night he sat on the floor of the shop beside the sidecar with far too many photographs on his phone. She was cleaning tools.

“Jia? Would you make another one?”

“Why?”

“For the tram.”

She laughed so hard she dropped the cloth. “A sidecar. On a bike that does twenty.”

“Possibly.”

She came and sat down beside him and he leaned his shoulder on hers.

“Do you remember the first time?” she said. “You were kneeling in the middle of a race.”

“I was.”

“And now you’re sitting in a sidecar.”

“An improvement.”

He kissed her hair. “I love you.”

Her face went soft. “I know.” Then she took his hand, and said, very quietly, “I love you too.”

He went completely still.

“What?” she said. “Your face is doing something.”

“Sorry.”

“Don’t be,” said Jinx, and kissed him.

He’d spent his life looking at buildings for where they’d fail. The cracks. The distances. The ways out. That night he looked round the shop under its new roof and saw something else: a woman who built things that worked, a life that wasn’t hidden, and a seat beside her, made for him.

chapters.title: Raiden Is Proud of Her for an Entire Week
chapters.desc: Her black bike wins Best in Show up north, and her husband tells a petrol station, a toll booth and a coach party. He tells everyone except his own family.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d like everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.”
chapters.content:
Raiden entered the motorbike without telling Jinx.

In his opinion this was perfectly reasonable. He hadn’t entered her without permission. He’d entered the bike. There was a difference.

The bike was called Carp. She’d named it years ago, after a customer had stood in the shop and insisted that a motorbike had to be red, because red was the colour of speed, and she’d told him that if he wanted a fish he should buy one. The customer left. The bike stayed black: a deep, nearly liquid black with graphite under it, the tank shaped to follow the frame instead of shouting over it, an exhaust she’d bent herself, and not one bracket or weld or setting on it that didn’t have a reason. It wasn’t the most expensive thing in the shop, or the most powerful. It was the only one she’d ever built without a client to argue with.

He loved it. He loved the woman who’d built it. And he had decided the Northern Custom Show should see both.

Category: Custom Motorcycle. Entrant: Cao Jia. Machine: Carp. He arranged the transport, paid the fee, read the regulations twice, booked a room near the hall, and wrote the description for the card:

Built and engineered by Cao Jia. A study in restraint, mechanical balance, and the beauty of a machine that knows exactly what it is.

She would have objected to the last part. Which was why he didn’t show her. He made only one mistake: he left the confirmation open on his laptop. On the evening of Wednesday the fifth of October she went looking for a supplier’s invoice for a set of brake lines and found the show’s logo instead.

When he came out of the kitchen with two bowls, she turned the screen round.

“I entered Carp in the Northern Custom Show,” he said.

“Without telling me.”

“Yes.”

She read the last line aloud. “A machine that knows exactly what it is.”

“I thought it was accurate.”

“Why?”

He put the bowls down. “Because it’s beautiful. Because you built it. And because I think people should see what you can do.” She folded her arms, and he didn’t look away. “I know you don’t build things for applause. I know you don’t need a trophy to tell you your work’s good. I just think you deserve to have people look at it properly.”

It was easier when people admired the finished bike. It was much harder when he looked at it and saw her.

“When?”

“Saturday week.”

“You’ve paid.”

“Yes. And the van’s booked, and there’s a room.”

“I’m paying my own costs. And I’m not wearing a dress.”

“I’d never expect you to.”

She picked up a bowl. “Fine.”

He tried not to look pleased and failed completely, and she pointed her chopsticks at him. “You can thank me for not throwing the laptop at you. There’s still time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The hall was three hours north, an exhibition shed on a ring road, and it smelt of polish and tyre rubber and coffee. There were bikes everywhere: immaculate restorations, elaborate customs, machines whose owners had plainly spent more on chrome than most people spent on a car. Carp went into her bay under good lights, and Jinx straightened the front wheel and checked the stand and rubbed one fingerprint off the tank with her sleeve, and stepped back.

“Ready?”

“Ready.”

For the next hour he behaved himself. Mostly. He didn’t touch the bike. He didn’t answer for her. He didn’t explain the engine when people asked. He stood a little way off, fetched coffee, and watched her talk: the frame, the intake, the exhaust routing, the suspension, why the weight sat where it did and why she’d kept the bodywork quiet. A man asked if the black was meant to make it look expensive.

“No.”

“Then what?”

“Black.”

Raiden coughed into his hand. He loved the way she talked when a question was worth answering. Her hands moved when she described a part. Her eyes went sharp when she corrected someone. She didn’t perform knowing things. She just knew them. He was so proud he thought his chest might actually hurt.

The rival came just before judging. His name was Victor Cheng, and his bike sat two rows away, huge and chromed, with bodywork like a wedding cake and a price that Jinx suspected would buy a small flat. He walked round Carp with two friends.

“Interesting. Very understated.” A pause. “Almost unfinished. A personal project? That explains it. Good luck. These things tend to reward more substantial work.”

Jinx’s face didn’t change. Raiden’s did, a little. He stepped up, polite as a waiter.

“Could I ask what you mean by substantial?”

“Engineering. Fabrication. Complexity.”

“Of course.” Raiden glanced along the row at the chrome. “It’s only that the hall’s rules say a quarter of a tank at most, filler cap sealed, battery off. Yours is full to the neck. I could smell it from the aisle. And the battery’s still connected, I think, because you want to start it for the judges.” He smiled. “It may be fine. I’m not saying it isn’t. I’m suggesting we have lunch with the fire officer. We could all learn something.”

Victor stared at him. One of his friends looked at the tank. Victor said something under his breath and walked off, and ten minutes later a steward with a clipboard and a roll of tape was standing beside the chrome bike, and Victor was draining fuel into a can in the car park.

Jinx was watching her husband as if she hadn’t decided whether to be impressed or annoyed.

“You’re mean,” she said.

“Only when necessary.”

“Don’t start a fight.”

“I didn’t.”

“You threatened him with lunch.”

“An educational lunch,” he said, and went back to standing beside her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The judging took nearly two hours. The rear suspension. The frame. The electrics. One judge asked why she hadn’t used more decoration, and she looked at Carp. “Because the shape already works. I didn’t want to add things just to prove I’d made it.” The judge nodded slowly and wrote something down. Raiden didn’t say a word. Once she glanced across and he smiled at her, and she rolled her eyes, and her mouth went soft anyway.

When they read the awards out, he held her hand and she could feel his thumb going back and forth over her knuckles.

“You’re nervous,” she whispered.

“I have less control over the outcome than you do.”

Best in Show came last. The presenter opened the envelope and smiled. “Cao Jia, for Carp.”

For a second she didn’t move. People began to clap. Raiden turned to her, and all the careful composure had gone off his face and he looked about fifteen. “Jia.”

“That’s me.”

“Yes.”

Then he took her by the waist and swung her clean off her feet, and a laugh came out of her she didn’t recognise, and he put her down and kissed her right there, in front of the stage and the judges and the whole hall, as if the prize had been handed to both of them.

“You won,” he said.

“We won.”

“No. You.”

The plaque said BEST IN SHOW — CARP — CAO JIA. She looked at it, and then she smiled, wide and with nothing guarding it, and he thought he had never seen anything as beautiful in his life.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told the petrol station first.

“Excuse me,” he said to the man at the till. “My wife won Best in Show today.” Jinx, behind him, closed her eyes. “Would you like to see the bike? She built it. From the frame up.”

“Raiden,” she said. “Pay.”

He told the woman in the toll booth, who said, “Congratulations?” as if it were a question. He told a coach party at a rest stop in the dark, while Jinx was buying water, and when she came back there were seven people round his phone looking at Carp, and one of them wanted to know if she’d build him one, and another’s nephew liked motorbikes, and as they boarded a man gave Raiden a thumbs up and shouted, “Good wife!”

“Very good,” Raiden called back.

She took him by the sleeve and towed him to the van. “You told an entire coach.”

“Not the entire coach.”

“How many?”

“Seven. Possibly eight.”

“You can’t tell every stranger in the country.”

“Why not?” He looked honestly puzzled. “I’d like everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.”

She sighed, and took his hand, and drove.

He sent a photograph to Mrs. Tong, who replied with seventeen exclamation marks and a voice message nearly two minutes long. He told the man at the coffee counter. He told a small boy who’d been staring at the trophy. But he didn’t tell Lin Jian, and he didn’t tell Elowen, and he didn’t send the picture to the family chat, and that was the part Jinx noticed, because she knew how much he wanted to.

Their marriage hadn’t been announced. He’d agreed to her terms on a napkin a year before: no family ceremony, no introductions, nothing in the Walled City. She’d never asked him to be ashamed. She’d only asked him not to drag their marriage into a world she hadn’t chosen. And he’d kept his word.

It was past eleven and she didn’t drive tired, so they stopped at a roadside hotel with a buzzing sign. She came out of the shower and found him sitting on the edge of the bed with his phone, and a message on the screen.

Elowen, Jia won Best in Show today. Carp took the top prize. I wish you could have seen her face—

He looked at it for a long time. Then he deleted it.

He hadn’t seen her in the doorway. She came and sat beside him. “What were you writing?”

He showed her the empty box.

“You wanted to tell her.”

“Yes. And my father. I wanted them to know what you did.” He took her hand. “I don’t regret it. I regret that I can’t share every part of my life with everyone I love. But I don’t regret choosing you. And I don’t ever want you to feel I’m waiting for you to become acceptable to my family.”

“You’re not,” she said, and put her forehead against his.

“No.”

She took the phone out of his hand and put it face down on the bedside table, and then she climbed into his lap with her knees either side of his hips, and he made a small surprised sound and caught her.

“I’m proud of you,” she said. “For not making me fight you over it.”

“That’s a very low standard.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

She kissed him slowly. He was still in yesterday’s shirt, and she undid the buttons one by one with her eyes on his face, and pushed it off his shoulders, and put her mouth to his collarbone, and then his throat, where his pulse jumped. He pulled the towel loose from her and it fell away, and his hands came up her bare back and stayed there, spread wide, holding her as though she were the prize. She was the one who reached down between them. She was the one who lifted herself and sank onto him, slowly, a breath at a time, until he was all the way inside her and his head had gone back and her name had come out of him like something breaking. She rode him in the yellow light from the car park, unhurried, her hands on his shoulders, watching every change in his face, and he let her see all of it. When he came apart it was with his face pressed into her neck and his arms locked round her, and she followed him a moment after, his fingers finding her exactly where she needed them, his voice in her ear telling her she was extraordinary, over and over, until she laughed into his hair and told him to be quiet.

Afterwards he lay with his cheek on her stomach and she ran her fingers through his hair.

“You can tell me when you miss them,” she said. “You don’t have to pretend it doesn’t hurt.”

“I know,” he said, and this time he didn’t look at the phone again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday evening, at home, his phone buzzed once.

Zhao: Best in Show. Well done to her. Your sister hasn’t heard it from me.

Raiden stared at it. “How does he know?”

Jinx read it over his shoulder. “He knew about us the night you were in hospital. He’s never once told anyone.” She handed the phone back. “Don’t ask him how. He won’t say.”

He didn’t ask. He typed Thank you and put the phone down, and Jinx noticed that it was the first time all weekend his face had looked completely easy.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trophy sat on the workbench for two days while she decided where it should go. He suggested the shelf over the dyno. Too high. The office. It wasn’t an office. The living room. She threatened the bathroom.

On Tuesday night she stood in front of it with her hands in her pockets, and he came in with two mugs of tea.

“Maybe up there,” she said.

He looked at the shelf. “Good.”

“You’re still proud.”

“Yes.”

“How long are you going to keep it up?”

He considered. “A week. At least.” He stepped closer. “I was proud of you before you won. When you were building it. When you spent three nights arguing with the rear suspension.”

“Two.”

“Three.”

“Two and a half.”

“I was proud when you explained the frame to the judges, and when you told that man black was black. And I was proud when you won, because everybody else finally got to see what I see every day.”

She put her hand on his face. “You’re very good at making a person feel loved.”

“I’m trying.”

“Come upstairs.”

He’d run the bath while she closed the shop, with two towels on the rail and her soap by the tap. They got in carefully this time. Neither of them wanted another flood. He leaned back against the end and she leaned back against him, and for a while there was only the water and the rain on the roof.

“You know what I liked best?” she said. “You didn’t talk over me. You didn’t explain my own bike to the judges.”

“I was tempted.”

“Raiden.”

“I didn’t.”

“And you didn’t tell your family.” She found his hand under the water. “I know what that cost. You kept your promise when you wanted something else. You were proud of me without needing anyone else to know.” She turned her head and kissed him. “You’re allowed to be proud. You’re allowed to tell strangers. You’re allowed to tell Mrs. Tong.”

“She already knows.”

“You’re allowed to tell Zhao.”

“He knew before I did.”

She laughed, and settled back against his chest. Down in the shop the trophy sat over the dyno, catching a little light from the stairs.

“I think I’ll be proud of you for another week,” he said into her hair. “Perhaps two. And after that I’ll start again.”

chapters.title: Memes at 2 A.M.
chapters.desc: He sends her memes from the next pillow at two in the morning. Then he tells her about a freezer and eleven hours, and she works out what his steel room is.
chapters.epigraph: “You built me a freezer with the light on.”
chapters.content:
At 2:07 in the morning, in the week after Christmas, Raiden Lin sent his wife a picture of a cat falling off a table.

me trying to sleep after saying goodnight six hours ago.

Jinx looked at her phone. Then she turned her head. He was lying beside her on his back, holding his own phone about six inches from his face.

“You sent me a meme.”

“Yes.”

“From there. Your arm is touching me.”

“I know.”

“You could have spoken.”

He thought about that, and sent another: a skeleton sitting up in bed. me waiting for sleep to arrive.

She reached across him, took his phone, and put it face down on the bedside table. “Enough.”

“All right.”

Rain on the window. The old building ticking as it cooled. A bike going by in the wet street. She shut her eyes, and beside her he shifted once, twice, and turned on his side, and she felt his fingers find the hem of her shirt and hold on to it.

“Jia? Are you awake?”

“No.”

“Goodnight.”

“You’ve said that.”

“I wanted to say it again.”

She caught his hand and kissed it. “Goodnight, idiot.”

For a while she thought he might really sleep. Then she felt his breathing change, not into sleep, but into the careful, even rhythm of someone trying very hard to persuade another person he was resting. She knew the difference. She’d known it for more than a year. Raiden could sleep through a neighbour drilling concrete. He could fall asleep on the sofa with half a drawing under his cheek, or upright in the van after a long day. But some nights, in the middle of the night, his body seemed to forget that the room it was lying in was safe.

She turned over. His eyes were open, looking at nothing.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. Really.”

She didn’t argue. She moved closer and put her palm flat on his chest. His heart was steady. A little too steady.

“Do you want me to stay awake with you?”

He nodded. It was such a small movement that she nearly missed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 2:43 he said, “You know about the farm.”

She did. The chickens and the vegetable patch and the barn roof that leaked. Auntie Lan’s terrible soup. A dog called Architect who dug holes. Drawings on the backs of feed invoices. He’d told her all that on a Sunday in August with his plaster just off. He’d never told her much about why he’d been there, or about the end of it, and she’d never asked.

“When I was nine,” he said to the ceiling, “somebody came. I don’t know who. I never found out. Auntie Lan heard cars on the track, more than one, and she took me by the arm to the back shed. There was an old chest freezer in there. It hadn’t worked for years. They kept feed in it. She’d emptied it that week, I don’t know why. Maybe she knew something.” His fingers moved on the blanket. “She told me to get in. I thought it was a game, at first. She put a blanket round me and told me to be very quiet, and she shut the lid, and then I heard her drag a sack of feed on top of it so it wouldn’t look as if it had been moved.”

Jinx’s hand had gone still on his chest.

“The seal was gone. That’s why it didn’t work. That’s why I could breathe.” He said it as if it were a technical point. “I couldn’t see anything at all. It smelt of feed and old metal. I could hear them in the yard. Men. Somebody laughing. A dog barking, and the chickens going mad. I heard them in the house. Doors. Things being moved. And then somebody came into the shed.” He stopped. “Somebody kicked the side of it. Once. Not hard. Just the way you’d kick something that was in the way.”

“Raiden.”

“I thought they knew. I tried not to breathe. I thought if I made one sound Auntie Lan would be in trouble.” His voice cracked on the last word and he looked away. “I was very good at being quiet.”

“How long?”

“Eleven hours.”

The rain went on against the glass.

“I counted,” he said. “Mostly. When I lost my place I started again. My legs went numb at about four thousand. I was very cold.” He swallowed. “When she opened the lid it was dark outside as well, so it didn’t make much difference. She was crying. She kept saying my name. She lifted me out and held me for a long time, and I couldn’t stand up, so she carried me into the kitchen and made soup.”

“Was it terrible?”

A small broken laugh came out of him. “Absolutely.” He breathed in. “She left a lamp on that night. A little yellow one, on the table. I could see the whole room. She said nobody was coming back.”

“Did you believe her?”

He was quiet. “Eventually. A few days later some soldiers came up the valley to see what was left, and when they’d gone there was a tin of peaches on the kitchen windowsill. No note. Nobody would say where it came from. Blue and yellow label, cold from the window. I got it open with a kitchen knife and ate them one at a time and saved the syrup till last.” He almost smiled. “I thought about that tin for years.”

She opened her arms and, after a moment, he came into them, his forehead against her shoulder. He was taller than her and heavier, warm and familiar, and she could feel how hard he was holding himself together.

It came to her in pieces. The steel room behind the tool wall. The air he’d had checked twice. The emergency light on its own circuit. The telephone. The door that locked from either side. The hatch to the roof and the way across to the next building. She’d thought it was Raiden being thorough. An architect’s draftsman who knew the difference between a room and a refuge. He’d never once called it a safe room. He’d called it the room.

“Raiden,” she said. “Your room. Downstairs.”

He lifted his head a little.

“The air keeps moving. You can sit down. Nobody can lock you in. It opens from inside. There’s another way out.” She touched his face. “And the light stays on, whatever happens to the rest.” She heard her own voice go. “You built me a freezer with the light on.”

He stared at her.

“You made it bigger,” she said. “You made it so nobody would ever be shut in it in the dark.”

Something in him gave way without a sound. His face turned into her neck, and his whole body went tight as if he could hold it in by force, and she felt the first tear on her skin, and then another. He didn’t sob. He didn’t make any noise at all. He just cried, silently, with his shoulders moving in small hard jerks, and she held him with one hand at the back of his head and the other between his shoulder blades. She didn’t tell him it was all right. She didn’t tell him he was safe, as if fifteen years could be undone by a sentence.

“You’re here,” she said. “You’re here with me. I’ve got you.”

His fingers knotted in the back of her shirt.

“I’ve got you.”

He cried for a long time, and she let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 3:16 she reached for the glass of water and he drank a little and gave it back.

“Sorry.”

“What for?”

“Keeping you awake.”

She pinched his cheek, gently. “Are you apologising to me for being nine?”

“No.”

“Good. Because that’s ridiculous.”

She lay back and pulled him down with his head on her chest and began to stroke his hair. After a while she started to count.

“One. Two. Three.”

At thirty he opened his eyes. “What are you doing?”

“You counted in there. So I’m counting now. You’re waiting for something. I’m giving you something else to wait for.”

“That isn’t how counting works.”

“It is tonight.”

She didn’t hurry and she didn’t lose her place. When he shifted she moved her arm, and when he opened his eyes she kissed his forehead and went on from where she was. At a hundred and six he whispered, “You don’t have to.” At three hundred and twelve his fingers loosened. At seven hundred and forty his breathing slowed. By two thousand her voice had gone to a whisper. At three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine she stopped, and his eyes opened a fraction.

“Still here?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“Four thousand,” she said. “Four thousand and one.”

He was past the place where his legs had gone numb. He was asleep.

“Four thousand and six,” she said, very softly, and stopped, and lay awake with her hand in his hair. She thought about a little boy in the dark under a sack of feed, counting. A woman crying as she pulled him out. A yellow lamp. A tin on a windowsill that nobody would explain.

“You’re not there any more,” she whispered. “You’re home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke at 10:43 to an empty pillow, a window open a crack, and the smell of coffee and something frying.

Jinx: Breakfast. Don’t come down without a shirt.

Jinx: And no more skeletons.

He went down. She was at the stove and didn’t turn round. “Sleep?”

“Yes.”

He put his arms round her from behind and his chin on her shoulder. “Thank you. For last night.”

“You don’t have to thank me for holding you.”

“I know.” He held on a little longer, until she pointed the spatula at the table. “Sit. You’re in the way.”

They didn’t talk about the freezer for the next few days. Not because she’d forgotten, or because he wished he hadn’t told her. They let it settle. He slept better. Not perfectly. There were still nights he woke and checked the window, or lay too still. But now, sometimes, he reached for her hand. And sometimes she counted, and sometimes she didn’t need to.

On Friday afternoon she went into the shop for a torque wrench and found his legs sticking out from under a customer’s bike, an inspection lamp in his hand.

“You’ve got oil on your shirt.”

“The damage is done.”

“What are you doing?”

“Checking the rear mounting bracket. I heard a noise.”

She lay down on the creeper beside him and pushed in until their shoulders touched. The bracket was fine. “Then why are you still under here?”

“I like it under here. It’s where we started.”

“We met on a road.”

“Then it’s where you kissed me.”

It was. She looked at him in the narrow space under the frame, with grease on his cheek. He was smiling, and it wasn’t the careful smile he used to avoid questions, or the polite one he wore for strangers. It was small and warm and his own. She wiped the grease off with her thumb.

“I love you,” he said. And then, because she’d smiled and said I know, he said it again. “I love you, Jia.” No joke after it. No rule. He just looked at her.

She kissed him, slowly, and then again, lingering, until he smiled against her mouth.

“I love you too,” she said.

“I know.”

“Don’t steal my line.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she went down alone and unlocked the room. The door swung in without a sound. Steel walls. The fan’s quiet breath. The emergency light. The telephone. Everything exactly as he’d built it.

She went back upstairs for the little lamp from the bedroom, with its warm yellow shade, and put it on the shelf beside the emergency light. Then she took a tin from the kitchen cupboard and found him at the sink, drying two cups.

“Peaches?” he said.

“Come with me.”

He followed her down. When she opened the door he saw the lamp, already lit, and the tin beside it, and he didn’t say anything at all.

“It’s not much,” she said. “I thought it could use something that isn’t an emergency. And people should have something to eat. We’ll put a proper chair in. A blanket.” She took his hand. “It’s not a freezer. It’s not somewhere you have to keep quiet until someone decides it’s safe to open the lid. It’s a room. You can walk into it, and you can walk out of it, whenever you like.”

His eyes had gone wet. He pulled her against him and they stood under the yellow light.

“It’s the right colour,” he said into her hair.

“I thought so.”

“Can we leave it on?”

“Of course.”

“Even when nobody’s in here?”

“Especially then.”

She’d brought a tin opener in her back pocket, because she wasn’t an amateur, and one fork. They sat on the steel floor with their backs to the wall and the door wide open on the dark shop, and ate the peaches out of the tin, passing the fork back and forth, the syrup running down his wrist. He licked it off. She told him he was disgusting. He said it was the best tin of peaches he’d ever had, including the first one, and she said that was a very sentimental thing to say about fruit.

After a while she noticed that he wasn’t looking at the door. Every other time she’d seen him in a room, any room, a restaurant or a ballroom or a hospital ward, some part of him had been keeping count of the ways out. Now he was looking at the lamp, and at her, and at the last peach going round in the syrup, and nothing else.

“Have it,” she said.

“We’ll share it.”

She cut it in half with the edge of the fork, very badly, and gave him the bigger piece.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 2:07 the next morning her phone lit up. He was lying beside her, looking at her.

Raiden: [a peach in sunglasses] when you survive the freezer and finally get a room with snacks.

Jinx: You’re sleeping on the sofa.

Raiden: Is the lamp staying on?

She looked across the pillow. His smile was small and a little shy. She put the phone down and took his hand.

“Yes,” she whispered, and kissed him. “Now go to sleep.”

He closed his eyes, and this time he did.

chapters.title: Ten, Walking Home Alone
chapters.desc: How a boy of ten copied a road map onto his arm and crossed a border in a fish truck. At two in the morning she rides him to the red door in his father’s back wall.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody was coming. So I went to them.”
chapters.content:
He told her on a Saturday afternoon in the middle of January, not because he’d planned to, but because she was sitting cross-legged on the shop floor fighting a seized bolt on a customer’s bike, and she asked.

“How did you get home?”

He looked up from the drawing on his knee.

“From the farm,” she said, and gave the bolt another heave. “You told me once you walked. You said one day you’d tell me that part. You don’t have to. I’m only asking.”

He put the drawing down.

“I walked,” he said.

Her spanner stopped.

“I was ten. After the freezer it was never quite right there. Letters came. Auntie Lan wouldn’t let me see them. A man came to the gate one afternoon and asked her questions in a nice voice, and then he came again. She telephoned the city. I heard her in the kitchen at night saying yes, and I know, and how long, and crying when she put the phone down. Then one night in spring the man came back, late, and she took me out through the vegetable patch to the back wall. She gave me her old coat and the money out of the egg tin and half a loaf, and told me to go down the river road to the market in the old ferry town and wait by the fish stalls, and she’d come for me in the morning. And if she didn’t come, I was to find a police station.”

“Did she come?”

“I waited till the stalls packed up.” He looked at his hands. “Nobody was coming. So I went to them.”

“The police?”

“Home.” He smiled, not very well. “I didn’t want the police. I’d spent eleven hours in a freezer because of men who came in cars. I wasn’t going to get into one.”

He took out his phone and found a photograph. An old sheet of paper, yellow and soft at the folds. Roads in pencil, little arrows, a river, the names of towns in a child’s careful capitals, and symbols in the margins he must have invented.

“Auntie Lan kept a road atlas in a drawer. I wasn’t allowed to touch it. I used to copy it when she was out with the chickens.” He pointed. “The farm, with the water tower. The river road. The old ferry town. The border. And here.” He turned his left arm over and tapped the inside of the forearm. “The paper got wet when it rained, so I drew the important roads here, in biro. Every morning I checked. If it had faded I drew it again.”

She imagined it. A small boy in a coat far too big for him at the side of a road, studying the inside of his own arm.

“How did you cross?”

“In a fish truck.”

She shut her eyes.

“I know. There was a man loading crates at the market. I asked if he was going over the border. He told me to get lost.”

“Good.”

“I thought so too. So I climbed in between the crates when he went inside for his money.” He looked towards the roll-up door. “The cold wasn’t as bad as the freezer. The smell was worse. When the truck stopped I heard voices outside speaking differently, and knew we’d crossed. It wasn’t one truck. Six days. I got out when I could. I slept in places I didn’t know. A woman at a bus stand gave me a boiled egg. A man told me I shouldn’t be travelling on my own, and I told him my name was Ah Fai and my uncle was in the toilet, and ran.”

“Did anyone hurt you?”

He was quiet for a moment. “Nobody did anything I couldn’t get away from.”

There were a hundred things she wanted to ask. Where he’d slept. How hungry he’d been. Whether he’d cried, and who had seen. At ten she’d been under a bench in her father’s shop with a carburettor in her lap and men stepping round her, and she’d thought that was the worst place a child could be. She’d been wrong about that. She’d had a bench. She’d had a door that was always open, even if nobody good came through it. He’d had a road, and his arm, and a biro. She looked at his face and understood that the answers weren’t all hers to ask for. She put down the spanner, and reached across the bike, and took his hand.

“You were a little boy.”

“I didn’t think of it like that. I just wanted to get home.”

“To your father.”

“To my father.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tell me about the door,” she said.

“There’s a gate at the back of the house, in the lane. A red door in the wall. Ah Sim uses it, and the boys with the rice. I’d never been through it. I’d only ever seen the house in a photograph he brought to the farm at New Year.” He smiled a little. “I got there just after dark. The map on my arm was nearly gone. I stood outside so long I found a crack in the wood beside the lock and kept my finger in it.”

“Why?”

“I was afraid he wouldn’t be there. Or that he wouldn’t know me. He’d only ever seen me once a year.” He swallowed. “Then I knocked three times.”

She waited.

“I heard feet. The bolt. And it was him. I’ve never known why. He never uses that gate. He just stood there and looked at me, and I think he thought he was seeing things. Then he said my name. Not loudly. Just my name.” His voice went. “And he sat down.”

“Sat down?”

“On the step. As if his legs had stopped. He looked at my face and my clothes and my arm, and touched my hair, and then he pulled me in and held on. He didn’t ask where I’d been or how I’d got there. He kept saying, You’re home. Over and over. His coat smelt of cigarettes and rain.” He was looking at something a long way off. “And then, still on the step, he told me why I’d been away all my life. That I’d been sickly from the day I was born, and the city air was bad for me.”

“Was it true?”

“No.” He met her eyes. “I believed it for thirteen years. The real reason isn’t only mine to tell. Part of it belongs to my sister.”

She didn’t push. She knew enough about the Lin family to know their house had more locked rooms than his steel one.

“That night I made them all laugh at dinner,” he said. “Elowen thought for years that I’d been lucky.”

She got up off the floor, and came round the bike, and put her arms round his neck and her cheek on his hair.

“Take me there.”

“Where?”

“The door. Not the house. Not your family. Not anyone. I just want to see where you came home.”

“Jia. You said nothing in the Walled City.”

“That was about the wedding,” she said. “This is me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning the city belonged to people with nowhere urgent to be. She rolled the bike out with the green sidecar under the streetlamp, ARCHITECT on its brass plate, and handed him a helmet.

“I can drive,” he said.

“I know. Get in. I want to see your face.”

The Walled City was quieter than she’d expected, and never empty: lights behind old windows, a man smoking under an awning, a television somewhere, cables slung across the narrow streets, walls patched over walls. He directed her without an address. Left here. Straight. Not that one, the next. His voice had changed. He wasn’t reading the buildings for their structure. He was remembering. At the mouth of a lane between high blank walls he said, “Here,” and she cut the engine.

The red door was set into the wall at the top of three worn steps. The paint was fresh. The bolt was brass. Beside the lock, in the wood, there was still a small crack.

At the far end of the lane a man in a dark jacket stood under a light with his hands in his pockets. He looked at Raiden for a long second. Then he turned and looked the other way, as he’d been paid to do all his life.

Raiden stood at the bottom of the steps. He looked down at his left hand, and at the washer on it, and started to work it off.

She caught his wrist. “Keep it on.”

“If somebody comes out—“

“Then they’ll see it.” She rubbed her thumb over the ring. “You’re my husband. You don’t have to hide that from a door.”

Something moved across his face. He nodded.

She went up the three steps and lifted her hand and knocked on the wood, three times, very softly. His face changed as if he could hear it all again: the feet, the bolt, his father’s voice.

“Sorry,” she said.

“No.”

“What did you think, when it opened?”

“That I’d made it. Not that anything was mended. Not that I understood anything.” He swallowed. “I thought I could stop walking.”

She came down and leaned her shoulder against his. “Then you can stop now. We’re not going anywhere.”

He bent his head and kissed her. It wasn’t like the kisses in the shop with grease on their hands, or the ones at home while the kettle boiled. It was slow and careful, as if he were letting himself remember the door without having to stand in front of it alone. She held his face between her hands, and when he lifted his head she put her forehead against his.

“You’re home,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

They didn’t go at once. Across the lane there was a low wall under a shuttered window, and he sat on it and she stood between his knees, and he looked over her shoulder at the red door.

“Do you think he’d know me now?”

“He knew you at ten, filthy and starving in somebody else’s coat. Of course he’d know you.” She brushed her thumb over his cheekbone. “You’re still you.”

He was quiet. “I want you to meet him. Not tonight. Not until you want to. I don’t want you to feel that because we’re married you have to walk into my family.” He looked at her. “But I want it.”

There was no demand in his face. Only a wish. She looked at the door, and thought about the man behind it, whom she’d only ever seen across a ballroom with his eyes on her. The father who’d sat down on a step. She wasn’t ready. Not yet. But for the first time she could imagine a day when she might be.

“One day,” she said.

He went very still. “Really?”

“One day. Don’t tell them. Don’t arrange anything. And don’t buy a building.”

He laughed. “That seems unnecessarily specific.”

“Raiden.”

“I won’t buy a building.”

“Come on, husband,” she said, and the ring caught the streetlight as she pulled him up. “Home.”

She took the long way, down out of the old streets and along the harbour, where the water was black and the cranes stood over it with their red lights blinking. She kept the bike at forty and the sidecar ran true beside her. Every time she looked across, he was already looking at her. At the lights by the ferry pier he leaned over the edge of the chair and said something the engine took.

“What?”

“Thank you for knocking,” he said, louder.

The lights changed. She didn’t answer. She put her hand out instead, flat on the top of his helmet for a second, the way you’d steady something you’d built, and then she let the clutch out and took them home.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thirteenth napkin since January last year came with breakfast. He drew it opposite her while she drank her coffee: a wall, three steps, a red door with a crack beside the lock, standing open. A small boy outside. A man in the doorway, sitting down.

“Would you have a family wedding with me?” he said. “One day. Near that door. With all of them.”

She looked at it for a long time. It wasn’t a demand, or a date. It was a picture of something he wanted, with her in it, and a door that had once meant the end of a very long walk. She folded the napkin carefully and put it beside her cup.

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

“You knew that was the answer.”

“I like drawing you things.”

“You’ll run out of napkins.”

“I’ll buy more.”

She reached across the table and took his hand. “Maybe one day.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her ring. “I’d like that.”

That night he told her the old map itself was up in the flat on the forty-third floor of Meridian, in a box of farm things he’d never unpacked, and she said, “Bring it home.” Lying in the dark she asked what he’d thought when he first saw the red door, after the six days.

“That it was the most beautiful thing I’d ever seen.”

“Because it was home?”

“Because it was open.”

She lay listening to him breathe and thought about all the doors he’d drawn since. The one downstairs that opened from inside whatever the power did. The hatch to the roof. Every exit he counted in every room he walked into. A boy who’d stood outside a gate so long he’d found the crack in it, and had spent every year since making sure that no door he drew would ever keep anyone out, or shut anyone in. She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and left it there until he was asleep.

In the morning she found the napkin tucked into his sketchbook. Beside the door, in his neat capitals, he’d written: THE FIRST PLACE I EVER WANTED TO GO BACK TO. She took his pencil and wrote underneath, in her own scrawl, Not the last, and put the sketchbook back, and went down to make breakfast.
